section.title: The Righteous Branch and False Prophets
section.sectionRationale: Having exposed Judah's failed kings, Jeremiah now names the failed shepherds outright and answers their failure with the book's clearest messianic promise, a righteous Branch called 'The LORD Our Righteousness'. The chapter then turns to expose the false prophets who spoke comforting lies in God's name, pressing the urgent question of how God's true word can be told from human invention.
section.thesis: Where Judah's shepherd-kings scattered the flock, God Himself promises to raise up a righteous Branch who will reign in true justice and be called The LORD Our Righteousness, and He exposes the false prophets whose comfortable lies stand in direct contrast to His fiery, hammering word.
section.frameNote: Three movements: judgment on the scattering shepherds and the promise of the righteous Branch, an extended exposure of false prophets who speak dreams instead of God's word, and a closing rebuke of those who trade in the 'burden of the LORD' as a slogan.

verses.text: “Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture!” declares the LORD.

Therefore this is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says about the shepherds who tend My people: “You have scattered My flock and driven them away, and have not attended to them. Behold, I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds, declares the LORD.
Then I Myself will gather the remnant of My flock from all the lands to which I have banished them, and I will return them to their pasture, where they will be fruitful and multiply.
I will raise up shepherds over them who will tend them, and they will no longer be afraid or dismayed, nor will any go missing, declares the LORD.

Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous {{tsemach|Branch}}, and He will reign wisely as King and will administer justice and righteousness in the land.
In His days Judah will be saved, and Israel will dwell securely. And this is His name by which He will be called: {{yhwhtsidqenu|The LORD Our Righteousness}}.
So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when they will no longer say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought the Israelites up out of the land of Egypt.’

Instead they will say, ‘As surely as the LORD lives, who brought and led the descendants of the house of Israel up out of the land of the north and all the other lands to which He had banished them.’ Then they will dwell once more in their own land.”

units.label: Against the false prophets
units.note: dreams instead of the true word

verses.text:
As for the prophets: 
My heart is broken within me, and all my bones tremble. I have become like a drunkard, like a man overcome by wine, because of the LORD, because of His holy words.

For the land is full of adulterers, because of the curse, the land mourns 
and the pastures of the wilderness have dried up, their course is evil and their power is misused.
“For both prophet and priest are ungodly; even in My house I have found their wickedness,” declares the LORD.
“Therefore their path will become slick; they will be driven away into the darkness and fall into it. For I will bring disaster upon them in the year of their punishment,” declares the LORD.
“Among the prophets of Samaria I saw an offensive thing: They prophesied by Baal and led My people Israel astray.

And among the prophets of Jerusalem I have seen a horrible thing: They commit adultery and walk in lies. They strengthen the hands of evildoers, so that no one turns his back on wickedness. They are all like Sodom to Me; the people of Jerusalem are like Gomorrah.”

Therefore this is what the LORD of Hosts says concerning the prophets: 
“I will feed them wormwood and give them poisoned water to drink, for from the prophets of Jerusalem ungodliness has spread throughout the land.”

This is what the LORD of Hosts says: 
“Do not listen to the words of the prophets who prophesy to you. They are filling you with false hopes. They speak visions from their own minds, not from the mouth of the LORD.
They keep saying to those who despise Me, ‘The LORD says that you will have peace,’ and to everyone who walks in the stubbornness of his own heart, ‘No harm will come to you.’
But which of them has stood in the council of the LORD to see and hear His word? Who has given heed to His word and obeyed it?
Behold, the storm of the LORD has gone out with fury, a whirlwind swirling down upon the heads of the wicked.
The anger of the LORD will not turn back until He has fully accomplished the purposes of His heart. In the days to come you will understand this clearly.
I did not send these prophets, yet they have run with their message; I did not speak to them, yet they have prophesied.
But if they had stood in My council, they would have proclaimed My words to My people and turned them back from their evil ways and deeds.”
“Am I only a God nearby,” declares the LORD, “and not a God far away?”

“Can a man hide in secret places where I cannot see him?” declares the LORD. 
“Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?” declares the LORD.
“I have heard the sayings of the prophets who prophesy lies in My name: ‘I had a dream! I had a dream!’
How long will this continue in the hearts of these prophets who prophesy falsehood, these prophets of the delusion of their own minds?
They suppose the dreams that they tell one another will make My people forget My name, just as their fathers forgot My name through the worship of Baal.
Let the prophet who has a dream retell it, but let him who has My word speak it truthfully. For what is straw compared to grain?” declares the LORD.
“Is not My word like fire,” declares the LORD, “and like a hammer that smashes a rock?”
“Therefore behold,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who steal from one another words they attribute to Me.”
“Yes,” declares the LORD, “I am against the prophets who wag their own tongues and proclaim, ‘The LORD declares it.’”

“Indeed,” declares the LORD, “I am against those who prophesy false dreams and retell them to lead My people astray with their reckless lies. It was not I who sent them or commanded them, and they are of no benefit at all to these people,” declares the LORD.

units.label: The burden of the LORD
units.note: a slogan turned back on those who misuse it

verses.text: “Now when this people or a prophet or priest asks you, ‘What is the {{massa|burden}} of the LORD?’ you are to say to them, ‘What burden? I will forsake you, declares the LORD.’
As for the prophet or priest or anyone who claims, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ I will punish that man and his household.
This is what each man is to say to his friend and to his brother: ‘What has the LORD answered?’ or ‘What has the LORD spoken?’
But refer no more to the burden of the LORD, for each man's word becomes the burden, so that you pervert the words of the living God, the LORD of Hosts, our God.
Thus you are to say to the prophet: ‘What has the LORD answered you?’ and ‘What has the LORD spoken?’
But if you claim, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ then this is what the LORD says: Because you have said, ‘This is the burden of the LORD,’ and I specifically told you not to make this claim,
therefore I will surely forget you and will cast you out of My presence, both you and the city that I gave to you and your fathers.
And I will bring upon you everlasting shame and perpetual humiliation that will never be forgotten.”

tsemach.gloss: Branch or sprout, a shoot that grows up from a root or stump. Used here as a royal title for the coming Davidic king, it pictures new life springing from what looks like a cut-off, dying dynasty, and becomes a fixed messianic title, repeated in Jeremiah 33:15, Zechariah 3:8, and 6:12.

yhwhtsidqenu.gloss: The LORD our righteousness, the name given to the coming King, wordplay directly against Zedekiah, whose own name means 'the LORD is my righteousness' but whose reign utterly failed to live it out. Unlike the failed kings, this Branch's very name declares that righteousness before God comes only through Him.

massa.gloss: A word that means both burden and oracle or utterance, the same term prophets used for a solemn prophetic pronouncement. God plays on this double meaning: when people flippantly ask for 'the burden of the LORD' as slang for the latest prophecy, He turns the word back on them, they themselves have become the burden He will cast off.

basic.context: After exposing Judah's failed kings by name, Jeremiah now names their failure directly, calling them shepherds who scattered God's flock, and answers it with the clearest promise yet of a coming King from David's line who will actually reign in justice, called by the striking name The LORD Our Righteousness. The chapter then turns to expose false prophets who told the people comfortable lies in God's name, insisting that God's true word is like fire and a hammer, not a pleasant dream, and closes by rebuking those who casually toss around 'the burden of the LORD' as religious slang.
basic.hermeneutics: This chapter directly names its problem and its solution: failed shepherds versus a promised righteous Shepherd-King, and false prophets versus God's true word. The hardest interpretive question is how anyone could tell a true prophet from a false one when both claimed to speak for God; verses 21 to 22 and 28 to 29 give the honest test, true prophets actually turn people from evil and their word carries the weight and permanence of fire and a hammer, not the vague comfort of an invented dream.
basic.originalLanguages: God promises a tsemach, a Branch or sprout, springing from David's line even though it looks cut down, and this King's name will be YHWH tsidqenu, the LORD our righteousness, a deliberate echo and rebuke of King Zedekiah's own name, which meant something similar but whose life proved false to it. The false prophets are exposed through wordplay too: they ask flippantly for the massa, the burden or oracle, of the LORD, and God turns the word back on them, declaring that they themselves have become the burden He will cast away.
basic.typology: The righteous Branch springing from David's apparently ruined line anticipates Isaiah's shoot from the stump of Jesse, both fulfilled in Christ, who comes from David's royal line yet arises out of a dynasty under judgment. The contrast between comfortable false prophecy and God's fiery, hammering true word anticipates the New Testament's warnings against those who preach 'peace, peace' when there is no peace.
basic.christ: Jeremiah 23:5-6 is one of the Old Testament's clearest messianic prophecies: Christ is the righteous Branch who actually administers justice and righteousness, and He alone can bear the name The LORD Our Righteousness, since Paul teaches that believers are counted righteous only through union with Him, 1 Corinthians 1:30. Where false prophets offered cheap comfort, Christ is the true and faithful Word made flesh, John 1:14, who does not flatter sinners but calls them to real repentance.
basic.god: God is grieved, His own heart is described as broken, over corrupt shepherds and lying prophets who exploit His name for comfort rather than truth, yet He remains faithful to His promise to David even through their total failure. His word is not vague or malleable like a dream; it is as unbreakable as fire and a hammer, true regardless of how many false voices claim to speak for Him.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Corinthians 1:30 calls Christ our righteousness, echoing the very title given the Branch here. Isaiah 11:1 describes a shoot from the stump of Jesse, the same royal image developed further in this chapter. 2 Peter 2:1-3 warns of false teachers who exploit people with fabricated words, exactly what Jeremiah exposes among the prophets of his day. Ezekiel 34 develops the same shepherd imagery, judging Israel's failed shepherds and promising God Himself will shepherd His flock.
basic.oneStory: The failed shepherds of Israel expose humanity's constant need for a true King and a true word from God, not comfortable lies. That need is answered in Christ, the righteous Branch called The LORD Our Righteousness, whose word, unlike every false prophet's, is as sure and unbreakable as fire and a hammer, and whose reign will finally administer the justice and righteousness this whole broken history was waiting for.

context.literary:
Chapter 23 is a single speech built in four movements, each with its own heading. Verses 1 to 8 deal with the shepherds, verses 9 to 32 with the prophets, and verses 33 to 40 with the word "burden". The shepherd section is itself a small chiasm of woe and rescue: woe on the shepherds who scatter, 23:1-2, the LORD gathers, 23:3, new shepherds, 23:4, the Branch, 23:5-6, and the return from the north, 23:7-8. The prophets then take over the stage, and the ugly truth is that the second half of the chapter explains why the first half was necessary. A flock is scattered when its teachers say what it wants to hear.

The chapter is held by one word, repeated: "declares the LORD". The formula of divine speech falls about seventeen times in the BSB wording of this single chapter, and its density is the point. The false prophets are marked by claims of speech, "the LORD declares it", 23:31, while the LORD marks Himself as the only real speaker. The same logic explains the shift in tone at 23:9, where the first person suddenly becomes Jeremiah's own. The prophet's heart is broken and his bones tremble, so the true messenger is shown first as one overcome by the word, and then the false ones are held up against him.

Imagery piles up around speech. The false prophets feed on their own minds, 23:16, tell dreams like grain-thieves, 23:30, and pass around borrowed words, while God's true word is fire, hammer, grain and a storm that does not turn back. Straw and grain, 23:28, are a single picture of what is useless against what nourishes.

The passage also sits inside a longer unit on the royal house that began at 21:11, so the "Branch" of 23:5 is God's answer to the three kings of chapter 22 and to Coniah's curse in particular. The last movement, on the burden, is a pun that turns the chapter's whole subject, speaking for God, into a joke told against those who treat it casually.
context.historical:
The shepherd was the ancient Near East's stock image of a king, and Israel's kings were so styled, 2 Samuel 5:2. Hearing "woe to the shepherds", a listener in Jeremiah's day would think at once of the sons of Josiah and their officials, who had used the flock to feed themselves, as Ezekiel would also say, Ezekiel 34:2. The setting is the last years before 586 BC, after the first deportation, with the kingdom ruled by Zedekiah and the prophets of Jerusalem insisting that Babylon's yoke would soon be broken. Chapter 28 gives the most vivid example, the prophet Hananiah, who in the same decade announced that the exile would be over in two years.

Prophecy in Israel was a respected profession and sometimes a salaried one, and prophets could be paid for their words, Micah 3:5, 11. That helps explain the charge that prophet and priest alike were ungodly "even in My house", 23:11, and that prophets "strengthen the hands of evildoers", 23:14. A prophet who spoke comfort to the powerful was well placed and well fed. Jeremiah, who spoke the opposite, was beaten and put in the stocks, 20:2.

The prophets of Samaria belong to the earlier generation, the northern kingdom that had already fallen in 722 BC. Their Baal worship was a warning that Jerusalem's prophets should have heeded. The comparison with Sodom and Gomorrah, 23:14, was the worst comparison available to a Hebrew ear.

Dreams were a recognised means of revelation, Numbers 12:6, but Deuteronomy 13:1-5 warned that a dreamer could be a test of Israel's loyalty to the LORD, and Jeremiah's contemporaries had made a practice of dreaming and telling each other their dreams, 23:25-27. The word for "burden", massa, was the technical label for a prophetic oracle, and by Jeremiah's day it was a catchphrase people used in mockery, so the last section is a quarrel about speech in a city where everyone was quoting.
context.canonical:
The shepherd language begins with God Himself as Israel's shepherd, Genesis 48:15 and Psalm 23:1, and moves through the shepherd-king David, 2 Samuel 7:7-8. Chapter 23 belongs to a long prophetic argument that Israel's human shepherds have failed. Jeremiah promised in 3:15 to give shepherds after God's own heart, and Ezekiel 34 takes the same line to its end: the LORD Himself will search for His sheep, and He will set over them 'one shepherd, My servant David', Ezekiel 34:23. Zechariah 11 and 13:7 sound the same note.

The Branch is among the Old Testament's central royal titles. Isaiah 4:2 speaks of the 'Branch of the LORD', Isaiah 11:1 of a shoot from the stump of Jesse, and Jeremiah 33:14-16 returns to this very promise and applies the name 'The LORD Our Righteousness' to Jerusalem itself. Zechariah then gives the title to a man, 'My servant, the Branch', 3:8, and says that 'a man whose name is the Branch' will build the temple, 6:12.

The warnings about false prophets reach back to Deuteronomy 13 and 18 and forward to the New Testament. Jesus tells His disciples to beware of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing, Matthew 7:15, and 2 Peter 2:1 recalls that there were false prophets among the people just as there will be false teachers among believers.

The fire and hammer of 23:29 ties to 5:14, where God makes His words a fire in Jeremiah's mouth, and to Hebrews 4:12, where the word is living and active, sharper than any double-edged sword. Revelation 19:15 pictures the sword that proceeds from the mouth of Christ.

The exodus formula in 23:7-8 appears first in 16:14-15 and sets the return from Babylon beside the exodus as the greater act of rescue. Matthew 1:11-12 is the first page of the New Testament's own claim that the deliverer is born into that very line.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Jeremiah's purpose in this chapter was to hold two persons apart that Judah was blurring, the messenger and the word. The nation's leaders were comfortable because their prophets assured them of peace, and Jeremiah wanted them to understand that a comfortable prophet is not evidence of a favourable God. The honest test of any message is whether it lines up with what the LORD has actually said, and whether the one speaking has stood in His council, 23:18, which is to say, has listened before speaking.

He also wanted the people to see that their rulers' failure was not simply personal. A shepherd who scatters the flock puts a whole community in danger, and God would call him to account. At the same time he meant the hearers to hear, perhaps with astonishment, that the failure was not the end. The LORD would gather the remnant Himself and raise up a ruler worthy of the name.

Last, the passage is a warning against the quiet corruption of religious language. By asking for the burden of the LORD as though it were a casual phrase, the people had reduced the word of God to something to be traded. Jeremiah wanted them to ask the question God Himself gives them, 'What has the LORD answered?', 23:35, and to listen to the reply, even when it was hard.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes the false prophets of Jeremiah's day and God's judgment on them. Its commands are few and clear: do not listen to prophets who fill you with false hopes, 23:16, and speak God's word faithfully, 23:28. The condemnation is of people who claimed divine authority for their own thoughts, and the judgment on them is recorded as God's, not the reader's to carry out.

Care is needed in applying it. The passage does not say that every comforting message is false or every severe message true. Jeremiah himself speaks great comfort in this chapter, 23:3-8, and in the chapters that follow. The test is whether the message comes from the LORD, not whether it is pleasant or hard. For the same reason the passage does not forbid dreams or visions as such; it says that a dream is only a dream until the word of God stands over it, 23:28.

The practical lesson is the same for teachers and hearers. Those who speak for God must listen before they speak, and those who listen are asked to measure what they hear against the whole of Scripture, as the Bereans later did, Acts 17:11. The warning about the 'burden' extends naturally to casual use of 'God told me' language, which the passage treats as a serious matter.

debates.question: How could Jeremiah's original audience tell a true prophet from a false one when both claimed the LORD's authority?

views.label: The moral fruit test
views.case: Verse 22 gives a practical test: a true prophet's message turns people back from evil ways, while these false prophets, by contrast, 'strengthen the hands of evildoers,' verse 14, so their fruit exposes their falsehood.

views.label: The content and consistency test
views.case: Verses 28-29 point to the character of the message itself, God's true word is like fire and a hammer, weighty and consistent, not the vague, self-serving comfort ('you will have peace') the false prophets offered regardless of the people's actual conduct.

views.label: The test of fulfilment
views.case: Deuteronomy 18:22 says a message is not from the LORD if it does not come true, and Jeremiah 28:9 applies it to prophets of peace: they are recognised only if their word is fulfilled. This test is decisive, but it works only after the event, which is why the other two tests are also needed in the moment.

debates.bearing: The tests work together. Fulfilment settles the matter in the end, but while hearers are still deciding, the moral effect of a message and its agreement with what God has already said guard them against being led astray.

debates.question: Who is the Branch of 23:5-6?

views.label: The Messiah, finally fulfilled in Jesus
views.case: The Branch will 'reign wisely as King', save Judah, and bear the name 'The LORD Our Righteousness', language too large for any ordinary king. The New Testament announces that Jesus is given the throne of His father David, Luke 1:32, and that He has become our righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30.

views.label: An ideal Davidic king, partly seen in Zerubbabel
views.case: Zechariah applies the title to a man of his own day, 3:8 and 6:12, and Haggai 2:23 chooses Zerubbabel. Some read the promise as a pattern, an ideal king whose line is renewed in the returning exiles, with a more distant fulfilment still to come.

views.label: The royal line as a whole, renewed
views.case: Jeremiah 33:15-16 gives the same name, The LORD Our Righteousness, to Jerusalem, and speaks of the Branch as a continuing line. Some therefore take the language as describing the restored house of David corporately, not one individual.

debates.bearing: All three recognise that the promise names a David-like king who is righteous in a way the sons of Josiah were not. Christians read the title as reaching its full meaning in Christ, who is both the ruler and the source of righteousness, and the other readings show how the hope was kept alive in the centuries between.

study.originalLanguages:
Look first at the verb the chapter uses for shepherding, paqad. In 23:2 God says the shepherds have not 'attended' to the flock, and in the same breath, 'I will attend to you for the evil of your deeds.' The same word, to visit or take notice of, is used for care and for reckoning. A shepherd who does not look after the sheep will be looked after by God in a different sense. The word returns in 23:34, where God says He will 'punish' the man who speaks of the burden, so the whole chapter is framed by this root. It is the same verb Jeremiah uses in 29:10 for God's attending to the exiles to bring them home.

The Branch of 23:5 is described by the verb 'raise up', and the form of the promise is that God will 'raise up for David' a righteous Branch. The word 'righteous' is tsaddiq, so the Branch is a righteous sprout, one whose character is the opposite of the kings of chapter 22. He will 'reign wisely', a verb that carries the sense of acting with insight and therefore prospering, a quality David's house was meant to show, as in 3:15's shepherds who feed with knowledge and understanding.

The name in 23:6, YHWH tsidqenu, is built from the covenant name and a noun with the ending 'our'. The throne name of the last king, Zedekiah, means 'the LORD is my righteousness'. Nebuchadnezzar gave Mattaniah that name when he put him on the throne, 2 Kings 24:17, and it is an irony that the king's own name speaks of righteousness that his reign never showed. The Branch's name says the same words in the plural, 'our', which shows that this king's righteousness belongs to His people.

The false prophets 'run', 23:21, a verb of urgent haste, though no one sent them, and they 'stole' words from each other, 23:30. The council of 23:18 and 23:22 uses the word sod, the circle of intimate counsel in which a king and his advisers sit. To 'stand in the council of the LORD' is to be admitted to His confidences, as Amos 3:7 says. The question 'which of them has stood in it?' is asked with a sting, since the answer is none.

Finally, massa. It means 'burden' or 'load' and also 'oracle', from a root meaning to lift. The people use it as a label for prophecy; God turns the double sense on them. In 23:33 some translations read the clause as 'You are the burden, and I will cast you off', a play that the BSB's 'What burden? I will forsake you' catches in a different way. Either way, God's answer is a verb of casting off, the language of putting down a load and walking away.

typology.type: The Branch from David's ruined line
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah's Branch springs from a line that had been cut down, and the image of new growth from a seemingly dead stock is repeated in Isaiah 11:1. The pattern is life from what looks finished. In Christ it becomes literal: Jesus is born in the line of David after the royal house had faded into obscurity, Matthew 1:16, and He is called the Root and Offspring of David, Revelation 22:16. The type falls short in a way that shows its limit: a branch must grow, whereas Christ is also the root, the source of David's life and not only the fruit of it.

typology.type: The shepherd who gathers the scattered
typology.fulfillment: The LORD will gather the remnant from all the lands, 23:3, and raise up shepherds who care for them, 23:4. The pattern of the God who searches for His flock reaches its fulfilment in Jesus, who says 'I am the good shepherd', John 10:11, who is moved with compassion because the crowds were like sheep without a shepherd, Matthew 9:36, and who is called 'that great Shepherd of the sheep', Hebrews 13:20. He gathers into one flock, John 10:16. The correspondence is more than a metaphor: the shepherd lays down His life, which no earlier shepherd of Israel ever did.

The Branch is called 'The LORD Our Righteousness', 23:6. This name for the king has a counterpart in Zedekiah's own throne name, which spoke of righteousness and was not backed by his life. In Christ, the name is not a label but a gift: He has become our righteousness, 1 Corinthians 1:30, and believers are counted righteous through faith in Him, Romans 3:22. The type falls short because a name is only a word until it is carried by someone who has the life it describes, which Zedekiah did not and Christ does.

typology.type: The word as fire and hammer
typology.fulfillment: The true word of God is a fire in the mouth of the prophet and a hammer that breaks rock, 23:29. The Word made flesh, John 1:14, shows both. He kindled a fire on the earth, Luke 12:49, and His word searches the heart, Hebrews 4:12. The type is not a person but a pattern of speech, and its limits are those of every prophecy: Jeremiah could announce the word, but Christ is the word.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ most directly in its promise of the Branch, 23:5-6. Everything the failed shepherds were not, He is: a king who reigns wisely, who administers justice and righteousness, in whose days Judah is saved and Israel dwells securely. The name given to Him, 'The LORD Our Righteousness', joins the divine name with the gift of righteousness, and the New Testament uses almost this wording of Jesus. Paul says that He became for us wisdom from God, 'our righteousness, holiness, and redemption', 1 Corinthians 1:30. The God who gives the name is the God who bears it.

The chapter also shows Christ as the Shepherd. When the LORD promises to gather the flock Himself and to set shepherds over them, the promise looks forward to the day when Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd', John 10:11, and gathers sheep from outside the fold into one flock. The sheep He gathers are not those the old shepherds scattered but those He bought with His own life. His shepherding is the climax of Ezekiel's 'one shepherd, My servant David', Ezekiel 34:23, and of the shepherd after God's own heart, Jeremiah 3:15.

Christ is also the true Word, in contrast to the false prophets. They spoke a vision from their own minds, and He spoke what He heard from the Father, John 8:28 and 12:49. They told people they would have peace when there was none, and He was willing to say what no one wanted to hear, calling the crowds to repent. Where they stole each other's words, He is the Word who was with God and was God, John 1:1. He stood in the council of God because He is the one who made it, and He has revealed what He saw there, John 1:18.

And the burden of the LORD, which the false prophets made light of, is a subject Christ takes up with unexpected force. The invitation 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest', Matthew 11:28, answers a people who had been loaded with careless words. He carries the load that Jeremiah's pun says God will throw off.

The chapter's promise that Judah will be saved and Israel will dwell securely is also fulfilled in Him, Luke 1:68-71, and the return from the lands of the north that outshines the exodus is the pattern for the final gathering of His people from every nation, Matthew 24:31.

A caution: the passage does not predict the details of Jesus' life, and the false prophets are not hidden portraits of Christ's enemies. What it does is hold out a King who meets a need the whole book has been exposing, and then the New Testament says plainly who He is.
study.god:
The chapter opens with a God who is angry for His sheep. 'Woe to the shepherds who destroy and scatter the sheep of My pasture', 23:1. The pasture and the flock are His, and the failure of the leaders is measured against His ownership. He is not an indifferent sovereign who tolerates bad rule; He takes it personally because the people are His. That is a necessary corrective for anyone who imagines divine love as passive.

He is the God who gathers. After the verdict on the shepherds comes a string of first-person verbs: 'I Myself will gather the remnant... I will return them... I will raise up shepherds', 23:3-4. When the human shepherds fail, God does not abandon the sheep. He takes over the work. That is the doctrine of grace in shepherd's clothing.

He is a God whose word is real. In an age of pleasant dreams, He insists that His word is fire and a hammer, 23:29, which is to say that it burns what is false and breaks what is hard. The hearers are not meant to enjoy it as theatre. It does something. The image shows that God's speech is not merely information; it is an act that accomplishes what He says, as Isaiah 55:11 also teaches.

He is the God who is near and far at once. 'Am I only a God nearby, and not a God far away? Can a man hide in secret places where I cannot see him? Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?', 23:23-24. The false prophets spoke as though the LORD were a local deity who could be managed from the temple, or as though He had not noticed their lies. In fact He hears the very words, 'I had a dream', and counts them, 23:25. This is the passage's clearest statement of divine omnipresence and omniscience, and it is delivered as a rebuke.

He is jealous for His name. He says that the dreams are meant to make His people forget His name, 23:27, and the final section rests on the claim that the word 'burden of the LORD' is not to be handled lightly. The God who is not named carelessly is the God of the third commandment, Exodus 20:7.

He also grieves. The first person of 23:9 is Jeremiah's, but his heart is broken because of the LORD and His holy words, which means the prophet shares God's own sorrow at what is happening to the people. The anger of the LORD will not turn back until it has done what He purposed, 23:20, yet the anger is not the whole of Him: the same chapter promises that He will save.

For worship, the chapter calls us to bring the right posture before a God of such nearness and such holiness: not to ask for comforting dreams but to ask, 'What has the LORD spoken?', and to stand still to hear it.

crossReferences.note: The same promise repeated in the book's section of comfort: God will cause a righteous Branch to sprout for David, who will administer justice and righteousness. Here the name 'The LORD Our Righteousness' is applied to Jerusalem, which shows that the king's righteousness is shared with the people he rules.

A close parallel to Jeremiah 23:1-2: shepherds who feed only themselves are condemned, and the flock is scattered. Ezekiel carries the argument further and has God say that He will search for the sheep Himself, which makes Jeremiah's promise to gather the remnant a theme the prophets share.

After the exile, Zechariah takes up the title and gives it to a servant God is about to bring, 'the Branch'. The word is in use as a messianic name within a generation or two of Jeremiah and shows that the promise of 23:5 was being treasured and awaited, not forgotten.

The Torah's test of a prophet: a message that does not come true was not spoken by the LORD, and one who speaks in other gods' names must die. Jeremiah's charge that the prophets speak what God did not command, 23:21 and 23:32, applies this old law to the prophets of his own day.

Jeremiah's own statement of the test, in the confrontation with Hananiah. Prophets of old announced war and disaster, so a prophet of peace is recognised only when his word comes true. It shows how the principle of chapter 23 works in a named dispute.

The prophets heal the wound lightly, saying 'Peace, peace' when there is no peace. Jeremiah 23:17 repeats the charge in the form 'The LORD says that you will have peace', which shows that the false hope of the prophets was a long-standing habit and not a one-off mistake.

The word God puts in Jeremiah's mouth is made a fire, and the people become the wood. It is the earlier form of 23:29, where God's word is again compared to fire, and shows that the image belongs to Jeremiah's own calling and experience.

Jesus warns against false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are inwardly ravenous wolves. The tradition of Jeremiah 23 stands behind the warning, and Jesus' next teaching, that a tree is known by its fruit, supplies a test very like the moral test in Jeremiah 23:22.

Jesus claims to be the good shepherd who lays down His life for the sheep. Set beside Jeremiah 23:1-4, it answers the long failure of Israel's shepherds with a shepherd who does not use the flock but gives himself for it.

Paul says Christ has become for believers wisdom from God, righteousness, holiness and redemption. The righteousness named in Jeremiah 23:6 is here explained: it is not a mere title but something Christ is for His people, who have it through being in Him.

study.oneStory:
Scripture's story begins with a garden where God Himself walked and cared for His creatures, and with a vocation given to humans to rule and keep. When the story falls into ruin, one of its recurring signs is the failure of leadership, the shepherd who feeds himself. Jeremiah 23 is a vivid moment in that long refrain, and also one of its turning points.

The question the chapter answers from earlier in the story is why a flock that God has fed and rescued is scattered again. The answer is that rulers and teachers have led it astray, in the same shape that the serpent's deception took in the garden: a plausible voice that says 'you will not surely die' where God says 'you will'. The prophets of Jeremiah 23 who promise peace to the rebellious are the same voice in new clothes, and the passage's anger comes from recognising it.

What the chapter sets up is the hope of the Branch, one of the great strands in the Old Testament. The promise given to David, that his house and throne would be made sure, was not discarded, and it was renewed at the very moment the dynasty was collapsing. The 'days are coming' of 23:5 begin a series of such promises, in the book of consolation and in Ezekiel and Zechariah, that wait for a king from David's line.

The story reaches its centre in Christ, who is Shepherd, King and Word, and who gathers the scattered, and who becomes the righteousness of His people. His coming makes the exodus formula of 23:7-8 look small, because the deliverance He accomplishes is the greater one, from sin and death.

The end of the story is a flock without fear. Revelation says that the Lamb at the centre of the throne will be their shepherd and will lead them to springs of living water, Revelation 7:17, and that God will wipe away every tear. The promise that none will go missing, 23:4, finds its last meaning there. Those who have lived on the false hopes of this age will find that the real peace the prophets could only promise has been given, and the people who had asked for dreams will have what was true all along: the LORD is their righteousness.

sermon.title: I Will Raise Up for David a Righteous Branch
sermon.why: Piper works through Jeremiah 21:11 to 23:8, tracing the judgment on Judah's failed kings and showing how it resolves precisely in the promise of the righteous Branch named The LORD Our Righteousness, fulfilled in Christ, the exact movement this study traces.

quiz.q: What accusation does God bring against the shepherds in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: They have scattered and destroyed God's flock instead of attending to them.
options.note: The 'shepherds' are Judah's kings, judged for neglecting and scattering God's people.

options.text: They cared for the flock too gently and generously.
options.note: The charge is neglect and destruction, the opposite of excessive gentleness.

options.text: They failed to build enough grand buildings.
options.note: The accusation concerns care for people, not construction projects.

options.text: They were too focused on foreign military alliances.
options.note: The specific charge is scattering and not attending to the flock, not foreign policy as such.

quiz.q: What is significant about the coming King's name, 'The LORD Our Righteousness'?

options.text: It directly contrasts with Zedekiah's own name and failed reign, showing true righteousness comes only through this King.
options.note: Zedekiah's name carried a similar meaning that his life utterly failed to embody; the Branch's name declares the reality Zedekiah's did not.

options.text: It has no connection to any other name or king in the passage.
options.note: The wordplay with Zedekiah's name is a deliberate and pointed contrast in the passage's context.

options.text: It means the King will be righteous but will not help His people become righteous.
options.note: The name declares that righteousness for God's people comes through this King, not that it is withheld from them.

options.text: It is simply a poetic title with no theological content.
options.note: The name carries substantial theological weight, later applied directly to Christ, 1 Corinthians 1:30.

quiz.q: According to verse 22, what is the true test of a genuine prophet?

options.text: A true prophet, having stood in God's council, would turn people back from their evil ways and deeds.
options.note: This is the explicit test given: true prophecy actually produces repentance, not comfortable excuse.

options.text: A true prophet always tells people exactly what they want to hear.
options.note: This describes the false prophets condemned in the passage, not the true test.

options.text: A true prophet must perform visible miracles to prove authenticity.
options.note: The test given here is about moral fruit and turning people from evil, not miraculous signs.

options.text: A true prophet never predicts any coming judgment.
options.note: Jeremiah himself, a true prophet, predicts extensive judgment throughout the book.

quiz.q: What does God mean by comparing His word to fire and a hammer in verse 29?

options.text: God's true word carries real, unbreakable weight and power, unlike the vague, invented dreams of false prophets.
options.note: The contrast is directly with 'dreams' in the preceding verses, straw compared to grain, fire and a hammer compared to invented visions.

options.text: It means God's word is meant to be destructive without any purpose.
options.note: The image emphasizes the word's power and permanence, contrasted with weightless false prophecy, not destruction for its own sake.

options.text: It refers to a literal fire that consumed the temple.
options.note: This is figurative language about the nature and authority of God's word, not a description of a literal event.

options.text: It shows that God's word changes constantly like fire.
options.note: The image emphasizes consistency and unbreakable force, the opposite of changeability.

quiz.q: Why does God rebuke the casual use of the phrase 'the burden of the LORD' in verses 33 to 38?

options.text: The people had turned a solemn prophetic term into flippant slang, so God declares that they themselves have become the burden He will cast off.
options.note: The wordplay on massa, meaning both burden and oracle, is turned back on those who misused it.

options.text: God approved of the phrase and encouraged its continued use.
options.note: God explicitly forbids the continued use of this phrase in verse 36.

options.text: The phrase referred to a physical burden of taxation, unrelated to prophecy.
options.note: The passage is specifically about misuse of a prophetic term, not taxation.

options.text: It was a minor stylistic issue with no real consequence.
options.note: The consequence is severe: those who persist in the phrase face being cast out of God's presence.

questions: The false prophets told people what they wanted to hear rather than what was true. Where are you tempted to seek out comfortable words rather than God's actual truth?
The true test of a prophet was whether the message turned people from evil, verse 22. Does the teaching or content you consume actually call you toward repentance, or only toward comfort?

The righteous Branch is named 'The LORD Our Righteousness', our righteousness comes from Him, not from ourselves. Where are you still trying to establish your own righteousness rather than receiving His?
God's word is like fire and a hammer, unbreakable and weighty. How does that shape the way you receive Scripture when it confronts rather than comforts you?
The people had turned reverent language into casual slogans, 'the burden of the LORD'. Is there language about God or His word that you use carelessly rather than with the weight it deserves?

translationNotes.note: 'Righteous Branch', tsemach, becomes a fixed messianic title, repeated in Jeremiah 33:15 and developed further in Zechariah 3:8 and 6:12, always describing new royal life springing from David's apparently ruined line.

'The LORD Our Righteousness', YHWH tsidqenu, deliberately echoes and contrasts with the name Zedekiah, which carries a similar meaning; the King's name declares what the failed king's name only promised.

'Burden', massa, is the same Hebrew word regularly used elsewhere for a solemn prophetic 'oracle' or 'utterance'; the wordplay is largely lost in English translation, God turns the people's flippant slang back on them as a genuine, weighty pronouncement of judgment.
